https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-could-ex-d.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JFV2 Mykhailo Fedorov in the video address he published on his YouTube channel on August 18 Image: Mykhailo Fedorov/YouTube/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement This week, Ukraine was rocked by a series of political scandals. A month after stepping down as defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov addressed the Ukrainian people in a nine-minute speech posted on his YouTube channel. In his video message, he declares that Ukraine "cannot remain without a fully appointed minister of defense." But, he continues, "the main problem goes much deeper than one position or one ministry." He says Ukraine's greatest challenge is a "systemic crisis of governance," of which corruption is only a symptom. Fedorov also criticized the fact that no national elections have been held in Ukraine since 2019. A few hours earlier, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , had proposed Yevhenii Khmara to parliament as the new defense minister. Khmara had been made acting minister of defense on July 20, and parliament confirmed him in the position on August 19. Yevhenii Khmara attends a session of the Ukrainian parliament on August 19, when he was appointed minister of defense Image: REUTERS Corruption scandal involving public authorities When Fedorov spoke of corruption in government authorities, he may not have known about the scandal that would break the very day after he published his speech. On August 19, Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators searched the premises of several high-ranking officials, including a presidential deputy chief of staff, Iryna Mudra, and a member of parliament, Vadym Stolar. Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) stated that it was "conducting a special operation to expose a criminal organization" in conjunction with the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office. According to the investigating authorities, this organization was led by a current and a former Ukrainian lawmaker, and involved senior officials from the president's office. Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed Mudra from her post as presidential deputy chief of staff the same day. In his video, Mykhailo Fedorov warns that "it is especially dangerous when society feels that the main criterion for appointing a person is not their professionalism, results, or ability […] but their personal loyalty to the system." He says that a "legal, safe, and realistic mechanism" needs to be found to make it possible to hold elections, even if Russia's war against Ukraine continues for a long time. Ukraine's constitution forbids elections in time of war The president dismissed Fedorov from his post as defense minister on July 15. Protests calling for his reinstatement began the following day in Kyiv, Lviv, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and other cities. According to polls conducted by the Rating opinion research institute on July 20 and 21, trust in the ex-minister rose from 35% to 65% in the first week of the protests. Of the respondents, 72% thought Fedorov should not have been sacked. Thousands demonstrated in cities around Ukraine to protest the dismissal of Fedorov as defense minister Image: Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu/picture alliance A poll conducted on August 5 and 6 showed Fedorov in third place in the presidential ratings, on 12.5%. Volodymyr Zelenskyy led with 25.2%, followed by Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the former commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian army, on 16.7%. Ihor Chalenko, a political scientist from the Center for Analysis and Strategies in Kyiv, says Fedorov's address was an attempt to consolidate the political capital he won during the protests. Even though Fedorov does not present a full election program in his video, Chalenko thinks he is calculating on positioning himself as an independent political player who could stand against Volodymyr Zelenskyy. "For 35 days, people were out on the street. The demonstrations started with the demand that Fedorov be reinstated as minister of defense. But the fear is that the spotlight has moved on from Fedorov, because the protest campaign became increasingly focussed on the fight against corruption and protecting the anti-corruption authorities. So the former minister has decided to position himself politically and secure the status he attained," Chalenko said in an interview with DW. No opposition to the president? However, Chalenko doesn't believe that Fedorov has shifted to "irreconcilable opposition" to Zelenskyy. While there is clearly a conflict between Fedorov and the president's inner circle, Chalenko doesn't see this as a permanent rift with the government, and he doesn't rule out a return for Fedorov were he to be offered a position. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not yet been directly challenged as the constitution forbids elections in wartime Image: Ukrainian Presidentia/Planet Pix via ZUMA Press Wire/dpa/picture alliance Oleksiy Haran, a professor of political science at the Kyiv Mohyla Academy, thinks Fedorov's remarks about elections and a renewal of the power of state send an important signal. However, he too says he sees no decisive change in opposition to the president. "We haven't heard any criticism at all of Zelenskyy," he told DW. Demand for elections and change Haran says Fedorov's speech expresses what the people want. Polls show that Ukrainians do indeed want a change of government. However, the political scientist emphasizes that there is a problem: "We agree that Russia cannot dictate to us when and how we should hold elections. But the question is: how should we hold elections if Russia continues the war?" He believes that in order to hold full elections a stable ceasefire is needed, at the very least, and this is precisely what Fedorov does not mention in his remarks. Vadym Denysenko, a political analyst at the Ukrainian thinktank Business Capital, believes Fedorov's speech is not an election campaign by one former minister but the start of a bigger political game. In a Facebook post, Denysenko describes two developments he is observing one month after Fedorov's dismissal. First, the social milieu he refers to as "Self-Help 3.0", which includes the anti-corruption movement, has found a political leader in Fedorov. Secondly, some of Zelenskyy's former followers have switched allegiance to Fedorov, and these, the analyst says, are now his strongest supporters. Denysenko appreciates Fedorov's comments as a contribution to the discussion about renewing the power of state. He points out that these are the same ideas Zelenskyy campaigned on in 2019. Even though Fedorov doesn't directly say in his video that he would stand in an election, the analyst is sure this is what Fedorov's inner circle is working toward. And, in his view, they have nothing to lose. "If elections were to be held soon, Fedorov stands a good chance of doing well," Denysenko says. "If there are no elections, they can strengthen his grassroots support, and further weaken Zelenskyy." This article was originally written in Ukrainian. https://www.ynetnews.com/article/h1u11pr.text: The unusual visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow this week has raised concern among U.S. allies in the West over a possible renewed rapprochement between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump strongly denied a Wall Street Journal report claiming that Ratcliffe had warned his Russian interlocutors against an attack on NATO. Politico reported that Ratcliffe instead urged Russian officials to reduce Moscow’s military and economic support for Iran. It is still too early to know whether Ratcliffe’s visit had any effect on Russian policy. But one development that added to the sense of mystery surrounding the trip was the unusual activity of UVB-76, the enigmatic shortwave station often nicknamed “Doomsday Radio.” The station began operating in the Soviet Union in the 1970s on a frequency of 4,625 kilohertz. Its official purpose has never been publicly disclosed. Over the years, theories have suggested that it serves as a military communications channel for transmitting messages to Russian units, or as a means of communicating with Russian intelligence operatives around the world. The station usually broadcasts a short, monotonous buzzing sound. Occasionally, the buzz is interrupted by spoken Russian words, numbers or combinations of letters. Western media have reported for years that intelligence services in several countries closely monitor its transmissions. According to The Moscow Times, the station’s buzzing was interrupted at least 25 times on Thursday, roughly a day after Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow. The broadcasts included numbers, words and letter combinations. Among the words reportedly heard were “waitress,” “spray” and “existence.” The last time the mysterious station was reportedly this active was on Feb. 12, 2025, the day Trump and Putin spoke for the first time since Trump returned to the White House for his second term. Even Kremlin-linked media outlets reported on this week’s unusual burst of activity. As far as is known, Ratcliffe met during his Moscow visit with his Russian counterpart, Foreign Intelligence Service chief Sergei Naryshkin. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin did not meet with the visiting CIA director. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addressed the visit Friday, saying the discreet nature of contacts between intelligence agencies should not come as a surprise. “The non-public nature of interaction between intelligence agencies, which traditionally work ‘quietly,’ should not be surprising,” Lavrov said. “There are rules according to which intelligence agencies interact, and there is nothing surprising about that. They conduct this work quietly. We diplomats also work largely quietly. But by tradition, we are obliged to say something.” After Ratcliffe’s visit, Moscow also stepped up its rhetoric toward Britain. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova warned Thursday that Russia could strike British military targets because of London’s military support for Ukraine. “Any British military facility and equipment in Ukraine and beyond may become a target for retaliatory strikes over Ukrainian attacks using British weapons on Russian territory,” Zakharova said. “Those guilty of war crimes, including against our civilian population, will be punished and held accountable for their actions.” Lavrov joined the criticism of Britain on Friday. “Britain plays the most negative role in the conflict in Ukraine, both in relation to Russia and to Western countries,” he said. “It has been this way for centuries. Britain has always had partners for the journey, not allies. The United States is no exception. They have always looked down on everyone to some extent. “All the conflicts that erupted in our region were imported from outside. It always came from the British and the Europeans. Always from Europe.” Baltic states prepare for cyberattacks and sabotage The recent developments, including Ratcliffe’s Moscow visit, have also stirred concern in Western Europe, particularly in the Baltic states bordering Russia. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia each maintain relatively small militaries and have long viewed Russia as their primary security threat. Their concern has intensified amid doubts over NATO’s future effectiveness and amid Trump’s repeated criticism of the alliance. Although Russia remains deeply engaged in its war in Ukraine, it still represents a significant military threat to the Baltic region. Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics sought to reassure the public, writing on X that the country’s assessment of the immediate military threat had not changed. “As for the current situation, the level of military threat and its assessment have not changed,” he wrote. “At present, the risk of a direct Russian invasion remains low. What is possible are various acts of sabotage, cyberattacks and hybrid operations.” Rinkevics said Latvia’s Interior Ministry, armed forces and NATO allies were taking steps to prevent such actions. “We greatly appreciate NATO’s political, diplomatic and military efforts, including those of the United States, aimed at strengthening regional security,” he said.

https://www.dw.com/en/poland-lifeline-fo.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O33M Nastya Podorozhnya was a 24-year-old Ukrainian graduate living in Poland when Russia invaded her native country in 2022 Image: Adam Easton/DW Advertisement Hours after Vladimir Putin announced his "special military operation" in Ukraine on February 24, 2022, Russian troops began attacking Kyiv's Antonov Airport close to the home of Nastya Podorozhnya's family. Nastya was 24 at the time and living in Krakow in neighboring Poland , having recently graduated from the city's Jagiellonian University. Alarmed by the reports coming out of Ukraine and fearful of what was to come, Nastya rushed back to Ukraine two days before the invasion to be with her family and help her sister and her three children cross the border to safety in Poland. Helping compatriots fleeing Ukraine Nastya realized she could use her experience of living in Poland — how to get a doctor's appointment or simply buy a tram ticket — to help the many women and children arriving in the country from Ukraine. Following Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, there was an outpouring of support from Polish people for Ukrainians fleeing the violence Image: Krzysztof Kaniewski/ZUMA Wire/IMAGO Poles were offering help and food at the border, but some people sought to take advantage of the vulnerable arrivals. "I spoke to activists engaged in anti-human trafficking and they said what was happening at the border in the first weeks after the invasion was like Christmas, Easter and birthdays rolled into one for traffickers because people were so easily trusting the volunteers," Nastya told DW in a two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow her organization uses to provide shelter to vulnerable women refugees escaping domestic abuse or trafficking. Hotline still fields 100 calls a months Named Martynka, after Nastya's youngest niece, the organization also runs a hotline. It has received more than 5,000 requests for help since March 2022 and now gets about a hundred every month. Her small team provides psychological and moral support in four languages as well as legal assistance and counselling. Podorozhnya's organization, Martynka, runs a shelter in Krakow for vulnerable women and children refugees escaping domestic abuse or trafficking Image: Adam Easton/DW "One of the very young women who lived with us for a long time was drugged by her boyfriend who she met as a teenager when she escaped the full-scale invasion and after years of relationship she found out that he has been drugging her and selling sex with her to other people" she said. Nastya said she was motivated to help partly because of a traumatic experience of her own. While studying in Krakow, a Ukrainian man tried to rape her outside of her dormitory. After a long and difficult legal process, during which police detained the suspect before releasing him, he was eventually found guilty of violating Nastya's bodily autonomy and given a restraining order. "This terrible, traumatic experience not only gave me horrible PTSD, which later on sort of helped me be empathetic and understand survivors with PTSD, but also it put me through the system of justice and how survivors are being treated," she added. Aid cuts and donor fatigue Since 2022, around 100 women and children have found shelter in the apartment. Her team's work relies largely on donations from international organizations. But cuts to USAID have led to increased competition for grants, while donor fatigue has forced the team to cut its one-to-one therapy sessions. EU debates 'only yes means yes' rape law To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Ukraine is not in the headlines anymore," says Nastya. "The international attention has moved elsewhere. For all of summer 2026 we have been running a very challenging fundraising campaign. It is so hard to convince people to donate to a Ukrainian organization right now. There is something called exhaustion, donor exhaustion, fundraising exhaustion." The UNHCR 's acting representative for Poland, Czechia and Slovakia, Jun Shirato, confirmed the difficult situation in the aid sector. Speaking to DW in Warsaw, she said that funding cuts last year have forced UNHCR to scale back its staff in Poland by two thirds, from 120 at its peak in the months after the invasion to 40 now. The UNHCR has now closed three of its regional offices opened in Krakow, Lublin and Rzeszow after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Its sole remaining office in Poland is in Warsaw. Changing attitudes to Ukrainians Nastya's fundraising efforts increasingly meet with online abuse, too. Attitudes toward Ukrainians in Poland have changed . In the months after the invasion, many Poles opened their homes to refugees, including Nastya's sister and her daughters. Historical disputes between Poland and Ukraine — in particular surrounding the role of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army in World War II — are fueling hostility toward Ukrainians in Poland Image: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/picture alliance The situation is now very different. Earlier this year, new rules restricting access to child benefits and free healthcare for refugees who don't work were introduced. In the first half of this year, reports of hate crimes committed against Ukrainians in Poland rose by a third according to Polish police statistics. Historical disputes fuel tension At the same time, historical disputes between Poland and Ukraine , have resurfaced, fueling further hostility toward the Ukrainian community , which accounts for more than three quarters of all foreigners living in Poland. In May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) , which took part in the murder of tens of thousands of Poles during the World War II, triggered outrage in Poland. Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelenskyy of Poland's highest state honor, the Order of the White Eagle. While Poles focus on the UPA's massacre of Polish citizens, many Ukrainians view the UPA and nationalist leaders like Stepan Bandera as heroes because they fought against the Soviet occupation after the war. A pro-Ukrainian demonstration under the slogan 'Don't Be Indifferent' opposing xenophobic attacks on Ukrainians was organized by the Committee for the Defense of Democracy in 22 cities across Poland this summer Image: Klaudia Radecka/NurPhoto/picture alliance "This week we are supporting a family of Ukrainians whose car was completely destroyed. No windows left in the car and with spray paint someone wrote 'Bandera people go back where you came from,'" said Nastya, adding, "I think it is so devastating and I've recorded a video about it. We have hundreds of comments there, of people wishing me death, wishing me to go back where I came from. It is very tough emotionally." Animosity stoked by Russian bots Nastya said the hostility is also driven by Russia using online bots to stoke tensions between Poles and Ukrainians. "They do not want us to be together, or to remember who our common enemy is. They don't want Ukrainian refugees to integrate or feel welcome," she said. Despite the strain, Nastya remains optimistic that she and her team can continue their work. "For some reason I am — and this is the weirdest thing. I love my job so much. I want to do this beautiful thing. I would easily send my mother, my sister, my best friend to Martynka for support. I know there are few organizations that could provide such wonderful help." Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan If you or someone you know have experienced any kind of gender-based violence, the website lila.help lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country in the world. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Students protest in Belgrade over voting arrangements for Serbia’s elections on Sunday, 7 October 2026. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters View image in fullscreen Students protest in Belgrade over voting arrangements for Serbia’s elections on Sunday, 7 October 2026. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters Opinion Serbia A gen Z protest movement could be about to oust Serbia’s strongman. Here’s why that will shake Europe Misha Glenny Student activists seem set to defeat Aleksandar Vučić at the ballot box this Sunday. The EU should never have written off Serbian democracy Wed 21 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 03.21 EDT Share H istory may not be about to repeat itself in Serbia , but it is beginning to rhyme. Just over a quarter of a century ago, Serbian citizens turned out to vote in large numbers to inflict a historic defeat on the then strongman in Belgrade, Slobodan Milošević, who was seeking re-election as president. He lost despite his extensive control over the media, the judiciary and the security forces. When he was reluctant to leave office, Serbs poured on to the streets in their hundreds of thousands, finally forcing him to go. On Sunday, a new generation could have the decisive voice in an equally fateful election, this time for the national parliament. Today’s strongman, Aleksandar Vučić, recently resigned as president to fight the election with the aim of swapping the locus of power from the presidency to the prime minister’s office. But Vučić, who has been in almost total control of Serbia for 14 years, finds himself on the back foot for the first time since he assumed power, just as Milošević did in 2000. Like his close friend, Viktor Orbán, who was decisively beaten in elections earlier this year, Vučić has felt compelled to pull out all the stops to halt the opposition electoral coalition, known as the Student List (SL). Unlike Orbán’s Fidesz party, Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) is unlikely to be humiliated in Sunday’s vote. Opinion polls vary widely – some giving the SL a lead of almost 10 percentage points , others suggesting the race is neck and neck. Pollsters also suggest that the higher the turnout, the greater the chances for the opposition. Some fear that the aftermath could even be violent. Vučić is throwing the kitchen sink at the campaign to skew the result his way. He has tightened his grip on the media by supporting a change in ownership of what was until recently the most important independent news group, United Media. Last weekend, 10 prominent journalists from its most important outlet, the TV station N1, resigned in protest against senior editorial appointments believed to favour Vučić and the SNS. N1 had been key in reporting the rapid rise in support for the student protest movement since it emerged spontaneously in November 2024 . Students first took to the streets when the canopy over the main rail station in Novi Sad in the north of Serbia collapsed, killing 16 people. The tragedy occurred just months after a Chinese consortium had finished renovating it in what critics claim was a corrupt deal. View image in fullscreen Mass silent protest outside Novi Sad railway station to mark the first anniversary of the canopy collapse that killed 16 people, 1 November 2025. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters At first, Vučić’s response was to wait until the demonstrations petered out. But despite various attempts to coerce the students to retreat from the streets, the protests grew throughout 2025 and 2026. In March 2025, during a 15-minute period of silence to honour the victims of the Novi Sad disaster, protesters alleged that police deployed a sonic weapon , the US-made LRAD 450XL, causing the crowd to disperse in panic. The government denied the use of the weapon and later the interior ministry filed a criminal complaint against one military analyst over his claim that a sonic weapon was probably used. The demonstrations have showed no sign of letting up in the past two years. The big challenge facing the students was how to channel the undoubted energy they generated through the movement into a coherent political force capable of challenging Vučić. The old opposition parties were riven by factionalism and lacking dynamic leadership. But this summer the students announced they had selected candidates to stand in a new formation, the Student List, including prominent academics, engineers, workers, cultural figures and students. Their straightforward slogan is “Serbia or the mafia”. Vučić has responded to the challenge by cranking up the nationalist rhetoric in recent months in order to mobilise the far right. He has welcomed the support of his neighbour, Milorad Dodik, the de facto leader of Republika Srpska, the Serbian entity in Bosnia. Dodik has long been regarded as Vladimir Putin’s main man in the Balkans and more recently has cosied up to Donald Trump , whose associates are investing in a gas pipeline with his help. Vučić, too, has been cultivating support from Moscow. Personal relations between Putin and the Serbian leader have been strained in the past. Vučić has been supplying Ukraine with a significant amount of munitions while playing his complex game of trying to balance friendly relationships with the west and Russia. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business Read more But with the gloves off, the Serbian leader has become less coy. Another sign of how seriously he views the students’ challenge was his decision to allow the recent nationalist jamboree of a state funeral for the man known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić, with the aim of bolstering his support among nationalists. If despite all this the Student List emerges victorious at the election, the shock waves will be felt as powerfully across Europe as they were when Orbán was defeated. Above all, it opens the possibility of a swifter integration with the European Union , a move that would be welcomed not just in Brussels but in London as well. Successive British governments are concerned that the Balkans represents the soft underbelly of European defence where Russia can exert significant pressure. Since Brexit, Britain’s influence here is limited politically but it has been active in promoting security cooperation across the region, with Nato and the EU. Student activists and their supporters have been disappointed by an apparent indifference on the part of the EU to their political struggle and a general perception in the outside world that Serbia’s democracy is a lost cause. On Sunday, they aim to prove them wrong. http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/.text: CALGARY, AB , Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Horizon Petroleum Ltd. ("Horizon" or the "Company") (TSXV: HPL) (FRA: HPM) (Tradegate: HPM) is pleased to announce that its wholly owned Polish subsidiary, Energia Karpaty Zachodnie sp. z o.o. ("EKZ"), has successfully completed the main flow portion of the production testing program at the Lachowice-7 ("L7") well in the Bielsko-Biala concession in southern Poland. The well has now been shut in for a planned 30-day pressure build-up period, following which the Company expects to finalise an initial production commercialization plan for the property. Dr David Winter, CEO of the Company commented: "The successful completion of the production flow testing represents a further significant operational milestone for Horizon as it advances its plans to bring the Lachowice gas development into production. We have accelerated plans to commence first production and cashflow through an Early Production Phase targeting the third quarter of 2027. This development objective is to establish power generation and potential compressed natural gas ("CNG") sales, subject to completion of the required technical evaluations, facilities engineering planning and design, commercial arrangements and regulatory approvals". LACHOWICE-7 FLOW TEST RESULTS Following completion of the nitrified acid stimulation program on September 23, 2026, the well was flowed back through temporary, on-site production testing equipment. The testing program followed the mechanical workover operations and the subsequent acid stimulation. Approximately 4,500 bbls of completion fluid were lost into the formation during these workover and stimulation operations indicating a highly permeable, naturally fractured reservoir. Production was initiated using coiled tubing and nitrogen to unload the well. The program comprised an initial cleanup flow period, a pre-main-flow test and a six-day main flow test on a restricted choke. Initial cleanup flow period A 30-hour cleanup flow period was conducted. The final recorded flow rate was 4.95 MMcf/d at a flowing wellhead pressure of 2,100 psi on a 24/64-inch choke. (Note: This is a short-term rate recorded at the end of the cleanup period and should not be interpreted as a stabilized long-term production flow rate). Pre-main-flow test The final recorded flow rate was 6.75 MMcf/d at a flowing wellhead pressure of 2,362 psi on a 24/64-inch choke. This was a short-term peak rate recorded over an eight-hour pre-main-flow period, on a larger choke than the Main flow test, and should not be interpreted as a stabilized long-term production rate. Main flow test Over the 6 days of the main flow period, gas flow rates initiated at 5MMcf/d with a wellhead flowing pressure of 2550psi declining to 2.5MMcf/d at a flowing pressure of 1900psi while on a 18/64 inch choke size. The average surface pressure drawdown was 25% based on surface pressure data. These results are in line with the Company's performance forecast for the L7 well and consistent with the anticipated performance from a naturally fractured reservoir. The well has now been shut in for the planned 30-day pressure build-up period. Analysis of the pressure build-up data, together with the flow test results, will be used to optimise the Company's understanding of reservoir characteristics and deliverability and to guide the next stage of development planning, including facility design and development drilling optimisation. During the workover and stimulation operations, approximately 4,500 barrels of completion fluid were lost into the wellbore and formation. To date, approximately 1,680 barrels of this fluid have been recovered, representing approximately 37% of the injected volume. The Company considers load fluid recovery an important factor in evaluating the well's cleanup and production performance. Decreasing completion fluid recoveries over the course of the well test support our prediction that the majority of this fluid will remain in the formation. Across all phases of the flow testing program, Lachowice-7 produced a total of approximately 26.5 million cubic feet ("MMcf") of natural gas, 170 barrels of condensate and 1,680 barrels of completion fluid. These cumulative volumes include production during the initial cleanup, pre-main-flow and six-day main flow periods. The results provide additional data for evaluating reservoir performance and the potential for early commercial production. NEXT STEPS TOWARD EARLY PRODUCTION Based on the results from this flow test, the Company is now accelerating its efforts to commence an Early Production Phase targeting the third quarter of 2027. The commercialization strategy objective is to establish initial electricity sales through a gas to power facility while proceeding with plans for full scale field development. The planned commercialization strategy also includes pursuing opportunities to use produced gas for CNG sales. The timing and scope of the Early Production Phase will depend on the results of this ongoing technical evaluation, engineering and facilities planning, and is subject to commercial arrangements, financing and applicable regulatory approvals. Horizon will provide a further update following completion and interpretation of the 30-day pressure build-up data. ABOUT HORIZON PETROLEUM LTD. Calgary-based Horizon Petroleum Ltd. is focused on the appraisal and development of natural gas resources and clean energy opportunities in Europe, with the objective of contributing to European energy independence and security. Horizon is advancing its Polish natural gas assets through a technically focused, phased development strategy designed to unlock their commercial potential.
